what: Ralliant makes precision test and measurement instruments and sensors. It was spun out of Fortive in mid-2025 and owns brands such as Tektronix (oscilloscopes and electronic test gear), along with sensor and safety businesses that sell into utilities, aerospace and defense.
customers: Electronics and semiconductor engineers who test designs, utilities and industrial plants that monitor equipment, and aerospace and defense manufacturers.
money: Tektronix oscilloscopes, signal analysers and related software, sold to engineering labs and chip and electronics makers.
Sensors and monitoring equipment for utilities, industrial plants, aerospace and defense, sold mostly on long programmes.
moat: Tektronix is one of two or three names every electronics lab knows, and test equipment is sticky: engineers learn one vendor’s instruments and software, and a lab standardises on them. The sensor businesses sit inside customers’ certified designs, which makes them hard to replace once chosen.
risks: The 2025 loss of $1.22B is a write-down, not lost money: cash from operations was $398M that year. But a write-down this size says Fortive valued these businesses higher than they now look, and $1.6B of goodwill is still on the balance sheet.
Revenue drifted from $2.16B in 2023 to $2.07B in 2025. A spin-off that shrinks before it grows has to prove its plan.
Test equipment follows chip and electronics design spending, which swings with the semiconductor cycle.
As a newly independent company it carries $1.2B of debt and the extra costs of running its own head office.
opportunities: Trailing revenue of $2.28B is above every full year shown, a sign the decline has turned.
Free cash flow has stayed between $300M and $430M a year even through the write-down, about 4–6% of the market value.
Defense and power-grid spending are rising for years, and the sensor businesses sell into both.
Eleven analysts average a target of $81, about 29% above the price.
watch: Whether organic revenue keeps growing and margins hold. A spin-off’s first two years show whether the parent kept the good parts.
view: The headline numbers make Ralliant look broken: a $1.2 billion loss in its first year as an independent company. They are misleading. The loss is a write-down of the goodwill Fortive had booked when it bought these businesses, and cash tells the real story: $398 million from operations in 2025 and about $300 million of free cash flow over the last twelve months. What the write-down does tell you is that these businesses were worth less than their old parent believed, which is often why a parent spins something off.

So the question is what a steady $300–400 million of free cash flow is worth. At $7 billion the market pays roughly twenty times that, which is a fair multiple for industrial technology with recurring software and calibration revenue, not a cheap one. For the shares to work from here, revenue has to grow rather than drift, and the latest twelve months, at $2.28 billion against $2.07 billion for 2025, suggest that is starting.

The investment turns on Tektronix. Test equipment is sold into chip and electronics design budgets, and those come in waves; the AI hardware build-out is the best wave in years, and Keysight has been the main beneficiary. If Ralliant can show it is taking part in that cycle, a 29% upside to the analysts’ average target is reasonable. Until it does, this is a fairly priced spin-off that I would buy on evidence, not on hope.
bull: Tektronix catches the AI-hardware design cycle, revenue grows again and steady cash flow funds buybacks.
bear: The write-down was the first sign that these businesses are shrinking, and growth never returns.
